sections.text: Who is it who rules the spirit sacrifice in many; and at the time of death how may those who have learned self-control come to the knowledge of Thee?

The Lord Shri Krishna replied: The Supreme Spirit is the Highest Imperishable Self, and Its Nature is spiritual consciousness. The worlds have been created and are supported by an emanation from the Spirit which is called the Law.
The perishable nature of beings is called Adhibhuta; the divine Self is called Adhidaiva; and I alone, dwelling in this body, am called Adhiyajna, the Lord of all sacrifices.

We have completed discussion on Chapter 7, Gnana Vigana Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom. And well be entering into the discussion of Akshara Brahma Yoga, Yoga of Imperishable Brahman. So starting from chapter one, we have seen our own situation, the condition we are in.
We are fighting this battle of life, but we get confused about what is right action -- whether this is right or that is right, should I do this or should I do that? Constantly Im waffling between this or that and cant come to the right conclusion. So in chapter one, Arjuna kept arguing intellectually, but could not come to any conclusion. In chapter two, in the beginning he surrenders himself to Lord Krishna.
Then comes the guidance. So the guidance comes as the revelation about the true nature of our self. So in chapter two, we learned that all that which I have thought about myself was erroneous.
Myself is immortal being. And therefore once I realign my understanding about who I am, everything else will fall in place in a very new pattern. Just like when we are traveling and encounter a new road pattern, we have to adjust to it.
Unless you pay attention, you go back to the old way, and if you keep traveling the old road, you are going to run into some construction. So if I change the old way of thinking about who I am to the new way of thinking about who I am, then how I act will change completely. In chapter three, we learned the nature of actions, what actions are all about.
Actions are binding, but not the ones which are performed in the spirit of Yajna. So the escape hatch is that all my actions should be performed in the spirit of Yajna for the greater good, for the common good, which is Karma Yoga. So we learned that Karma Yoga is the way to act in this world.
And then what is Karma Yoga was defined? If you give up the anxiety for the fruits of actions, thats Karma Yoga. So now my goal is: I have to act in this world, but I want to renounce actions. So chapter four talked about how to renounce actions in knowledge.
Knowing that Im not the doer, Ill be able to renounce my actions. That renunciation of the sense of agency is sannyasa. In chapter five, we learned what Sannyasa is. Renouncing the anxiety of actions is Karma Yoga.
Performing Karma Yoga, I become a Yogi -- I become so efficient in my actions that I realize I am not the doer at all. And that is sannyasa. Once I renounce this sense of agency, then I have to identify with my true self.
So in chapter six we learn the techniques of meditation -- how to give up the identity with the limited self, the conditioned self which I currently consider to be me, and how to align with the true self that we learned about in chapter two. That alignment is chapter six: the techniques of meditation on the self. But now, how to meditate on the self? What is the subject of my meditation? We learnt that in chapter seven.
There we learned that the nature of the true supreme self is twofold. One is Lower Prakriti and one is higher Prakriti. The lower is the one which I can experience, perceive, feel, touch and cognize and say this is it.
So the reality which I can perceive through my senses is the manifest world. The Bhagavan says thats my Lower Prakriti. Everything that you see, touch, feel is made up of my own self.
The Asthatha Prakriti. Thats his Eightfold which is Bhumi, Apaha, Kham, Analah, Vayuhu, Mana, Buddhi and Ahankar. All five great elements.
Mind, intellect and Ahankal, Ego. So there is nothing left. You take any entity in this world, and it will fall somewhere in this combination of eight -- start recognizing my Saguna Prakriti.
This Prakriti has names and forms. But he says there is a higher Prakriti which is beyond this Saguna Prakriti -- the Nirguna Prakriti, which has no names, no forms, no colors, no attributes, no entity, no being. He said thats my Higher Prakriti.
That Prakriti is what Im now trying to align myself with in my meditation, because I can already identify with the Saguna Prakriti. So we started our journey from me -- being the most selfish person, only thinking about this is me. Then we expand our horizon and say, Im a little better than that; I identify with my family. I expand my horizon even more and say, no, no -- my community is also me, not just my family.
Then I expand a little further and say, no, no, my nation is also me. Then I go even further -- Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam -- this planet is my home. And then I say Im going to go beyond that.
And this cosmos is me. This gradually expanding my identification from this limited me to cosmic me. From a Saguna perspective is which I can do with my open eyes meditation.
But then I have to go to the higher Prakriti that is beyond all the names and forms. Bhagawan says thats my imperishable nature. Thats Akshara Brahma.
So chapter eight now attempts to explain what that higher nature is. In the last chapter, in the ending two verses, Bhagavan said that one who knows myself in its totality -- Adhibutam, Adhi Daivam and Adhiyagnam -- even at the time of death, even that becomes a glimpse. At the last minute this complete picture becomes clear to me: what is Saguna Prakriti? What is Nirguna Prakriti? And what is this creation is all about? So now Arjuna obviously wants to know all the technical terms he heard in last chapter.
So the chapter eight start with Arjunas question. And as we have seen, he asked Bhagavan to define seven terms he has heard in his discourse. What is that Brahman which you are talking about? Then what is Adhyatma Kim? We talked about actions we know.
Without action I cannot even survive. I cannot maintain my body. Then what is Adhibhuta? You talked about Adhibhuta in the last chapter.
Kim Proktam Adhi Daivam -- and what is called Adhidaivam? What is it that we call Adhi Daivam? Adi Yagna Katham Ko ata Katham -- what is Yajna and how does it work? Adi Yajna is Dehe asmin Madhusudhana. We have discussed Madhu Sudhana, the slayer of Madhu. Madhu was a demon in our life -- that which feels very good is my enemy.
I learned that in old age, the only taste that survives is sweet. I was talking to one of our friends who said, I dont know why, but I never liked sweets in my life. And now in my old age I like nothing but sweets. Isnt it very simple? All your taste buds die as you grow older. The only ones that survive are the sweet taste buds.
So the only thing I really taste is sweetness. Everything else is not very enchanting anymore. The slayer of Madhu is Madhu Sudhana.
O Madhu Sudhana, Prayana kale cha Katham Gneyo asi Niyatatma Bihi -- in the last verse of the last chapter, he said that even at the last moment, if you know this, know myself as Adhi Bhuta, Adhi Deva, Adi Yajna. How do I know even at the last minute? You tell me, how should I know? And how do I make sure that I will know? How do I live a self-controlled life? Niyatatma Bhi -- self-control so that I will know you at the last minute. He recognized that at least there is some exercise I have to do.
Not just relying on luck or chance that I will remember him at the last minute just because I named my son after him. In fact, he may distract me -- because Rama, Rama, O Rama went away from here to Austin, Texas. Im glad that I have only one son, and his name is not after any Devta.
Niraj! So Arjuna says, just let me know. All other six questions were relatively less important. What he really wanted to know about was the last minute -- that was the real question.
How do I live a self-controlled life so that even at the last minute I will know your real self? And why is the last minute so important here? Thats a milestone. When I decide that Im going to take a vacation, thats a change -- from here Im going there. Till that time, it doesnt matter; Im here.
Mawlik moving from here to Dallas, Texas. The day he moves is a milestone. Till that, he is just Mawlik.
So Prayana Kale Apicha -- because I know that I will have the transition from this self to that existence, how do I make sure that I go to the right place, to know you? The answer comes in the next two verses, which actually, if we wanted to discuss fully, could take six months. Well do it in the next 10 minutes. Aksharam Brahma Paramam.
Very simple. Brahman is Akshara -- that which is imperishable is Brahman. Everything that I know in this world is perishable. Brahman is imperishable. That means anything which I can assign a beginning and end is not Brahman.
Aksha Ra, that Akshay. That which makes I revel in that form is Akshara. Thats why the letters are called Akshara -- because they become real to us.
So Saguna, from that perspective, is Akshara. But Paramam -- Aksaram Brahma Paramam -- that which is higher than Akshara is Brahman. So from that definition, that which is greater than Saguna, different than Saguna is Brahman.
So now I have to negate everything that I know and go beyond my knowledge. Therefore it is transcendental -- it cannot be learned through intellect, cannot be experienced through my mind. It is transcendental.
Svabhava Adhyatma Uchyate. They ask, what is Adhyatma? It is Svabhava -- the nature of your own self. That which makes me who I am is my Svabhava.
Bhagavan Sankaracharya says that that which makes me who I am is Paramatma. When he resides in me, he is Pratyagatma. And when that Pratyagatma identifies with this body, mind, and intellect, it becomes the Jiva.
It is something between the Jivatma as I know myself and the all-pervading Paramatma. The part of him which is me is Pratyagatma. That is my svabhava; without that I cannot do anything.
Therefore he says, when I know my own self, that is Adhyatma. Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara Visargaha Karma Sanginitam -- this is a very revolutionary definition of Karma. From that perspective, Karma was always considered a ritualistic performance.
When you perform any rituals, they were considered Karma. From our Vedic literature, Bhagavana defines Karma as Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara. That which brings forth beings and things into existence is Karma.
So any creative endeavor is Karma. When I create something, it is Karma. When I improve something, its karma.
So anything else you do is just labor. Therefore nobody congratulates me in the morning when I brush my teeth -- unless you are a two or three year old child. Because its not karma unless I assign value to it and say I am doing it for the betterment of my teeth.
Then its karma -- Bhuta Bhava Kara. That which creates improvement and brings things and beings into existence is Karma. So Bhagavans Karma is that he creates this universe out of his self as Ishvara.
He takes the help of his Maya, becomes Ishwara, becomes Hiranyagarbha, and creates this universe. From our perspective, anything we do to create something, improve something, improve myself, improve the lives of others -- that is Karma. That which brings everything down is Papa, not Karma.

Arjunas seven questions in these verses reveal a fundamental human longing: to understand the ultimate nature of reality and our place within it. Before we can embark on any meaningful spiritual journey, we must first ask the right questions. Take time today to examine your own burning questions about existence. What is it that you truly want to know?
Krishna defines Karma here not as mere ritual, but as Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara, that which creates improvement and brings beings into existence. This revolutionary definition transforms how we view our daily activities. Ask yourself: Are my actions today merely labor, or are they true Karma, creative endeavors that contribute to the betterment of myself and others?
The teaching that Brahman is Akshara (imperishable) while everything we can perceive is perishable invites deep contemplation. Consider making a list of what you cling to most tightly, possessions, relationships, achievements, identity. Recognize that all these fall within the realm of the perishable Lower Prakriti. This is not meant to create despair, but clarity. The practice is to hold these things lightly while turning your attention toward that which cannot be destroyed. In meditation today, try to shift your identification from the Saguna (with attributes) to the Nirguna (without attributes), from the room space of your conditioned self to the infinite space of pure awareness. What would it feel like to expand your identification beyond me to family, community, nation, planet, and ultimately, the cosmos itself?
